extractions.quote: A 57-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital in February 2001 with symptoms of continuous muscle stiffness and painful muscle spasms, which began as tightness in the upper limbs and deteriorated into muscle stiffness of the trunk and lower limbs 1 month after onset.

At her first visit to our department, she was unable to maintain a standing or sitting position. She had no history of diabetes, injuries, or epilepsy. A laboratory examination and serum biochemical study including serum tumor markers also revealed nothing abnormal. However, another laboratory examination disclosed an extremely high titer of the anti-GAD antibody in serum at 16, 800 U/mL (normal range, /H110211. 5), suggesting a diagnosis of stiff man syndrome. The patient was treated with baclofen and diazepam, and her symptoms of continuous muscle stiffness and painful muscle spasms were relieved but were easily evoked by tactile stimulation. A computed tomography of the chest was conducted, which revealed an anterior mediastinal tumor that was considered to be a thymoma ( Fig 1), and suggested that her symptoms were caused by a paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome associated with a thymoma. We performed an extended thymectomy with wedge resection of the left upper lobe of the lung and a partial pericardectomy in May 2001. A histologic examination revealed the thymoma to be predominantly a lymphocytic type, which was type B1 tumor according to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification [6], with no invasion of the lung and the pericardium. A two-color flow cytometric study was used to evaluate the expression of CD4 and CD8 in the tumor-associated lymphocytes, according to a previously reported method [7], which revealed that 61% of all lymphoid cells were CD4 /H11001CD8/H11001, the typical phenotype of cortical thymocytes ( Fig 2). The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was able to recover muscle strength to enable her to maintain a standing or sitting position. She left the hospital 1 month after the operation; however, painful muscle stiffness returned 1 month later. Further, a head retraction reflex-like movement evoked by sensory stimulation of the face appeared, followed by severe bulbar symptoms with ptosis and dysphagia, which worsened and resulted in respiratory arrest. A tracheotomy was performed, and mechanical ventilation was required for 3 months.

extractions.quote: The chief symptoms of the disease are muscle rigidity and cramps, which are thought to result from immunemediated inhibition of catecholamine excitatory and raminobutyric acidergic neuron function. Further, 60% of patients with stiff man syndrome are reported to have antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD). In some cases, this syndrome occurs in association with other autoimmune diseases, such as insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, Graves disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and pernicious anemia, whereas in others, the disease shows a paraneoplastic nature with manifestations of breast cancer, mediastinal tumors, thymoma, small cell lung cancer, Hodgkin disease, and colon cancer [2]. Herein we report a case of stiff man syndrome with a thymoma and also review three cases reported previously [3–5]. A 57-year-old woman was admitted to our hospital in February 2001 with symptoms of continuous muscle stiffness and painful muscle spasms, which began as tightness in the upper limbs and deteriorated into muscle stiffness of the trunk and lower limbs 1 month after onset. At her first visit to our department, she was unable to maintain a standing or sitting position. She had no history of diabetes, injuries, or epilepsy. A laboratory examination and serum biochemical study including serum tumor markers also revealed nothing abnormal. However, another laboratory examination disclosed an extremely high titer of the anti-GAD antibody in serum at 16, 800 U/mL (normal range, /H110211. 5), suggesting a diagnosis of stiff man syndrome. The patient was treated with baclofen and diazepam, and her symptoms of continuous muscle stiffness and painful muscle spasms were relieved but were easily evoked by tactile stimulation. A computed tomography of the chest was conducted, which revealed an anterior mediastinal tumor that was considered to be a thymoma ( Fig 1), and suggested that her symptoms were caused by a paraneoplastic neurologic syndrome associated with a thymoma. We performed an extended thymectomy with wedge resection of the left upper lobe of the lung and a partial pericardectomy in May 2001. A histologic examination revealed the thymoma to be predominantly a lymphocytic type, which was type B1 tumor according to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification [6], with no invasion of the lung and the pericardium. A two-color flow cytometric study was used to evaluate the expression of CD4 and CD8 in the tumor-associated lymphocytes, according to a previously reported method [7], which revealed that 61% of all lymphoid cells were CD4 /H11001CD8/H11001, the typical phenotype of cortical thymocytes ( Fig 2). The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was able to recover muscle strength to enable her to maintain a standing or sitting position. She left the hospital 1 month after the operation; however, painful muscle stiffness returned 1 month later. Further, a head retraction reflex-like movement evoked by sensory stimulation of the face appeared, followed by severe bulbar symptoms with ptosis and dysphagia, which worsened and resulted in respiratory arrest. A tracheotomy was performed, and mechanical ventilation was required for 3 months. Although her bulbar symptoms were quite similar to those of myasthenia gravis (MG), results of serum antiacetylcholine receptor (AchR) antibody level and edrophonium tests were negative. In addition, electromyography (EMG) did not show a waning phenomenon, which suggested MG, whereas somatosensory evoked EMG suggested that her head retraction reflex-like movement was reflection of a brainstem disorder associated with stiff man syndrome, which might have also caused the bulbar symptoms. These symptoms were relieved after intravenous immunoglobulin treatment. Two years after the thymectomy, the symptoms and EMG findings were improved without medication, and the level of anti-GAD antibody had decreased to 9, 800 U/mL.

In the WHO classification, MG is more commonly associated with type B1 and B2 tumors than other types [9]. As noted previously, the three thymomas in the patients with stiff man syndrome were histologically defined as type B1 or B2. Type B1 and B2 tumors have abundant CD4 /H11001CD8/H11001T cells, which are supposed to have some association with the onset of MG. In our case, two-color flow cytometric analysis revealed an abundance of CD4/H11001CD8/H11001T cells in the tumor. These findings seem to suggest that an autoimmune mechanism of stiff man syndrome with a thymoma may be similar to that of MG with a thymoma. In the paraneoplastic stiff man syndrome associated with breast cancer, small cell lung cancer, Hodgkin disease, and colon cancer, neurologic symptoms have been shown to be relieved after tumor treatment [2]. I n the three resected cases mentioned previously, the symptoms of stiff man syndrome with a thymoma were alleviated after a thymectomy. Therefore, a thymectomy is considered to be effective treatment of stiff man syndrome with a thymoma.
